title: When a more cyclic majority tournament is more probable
shortTitle: A more cyclic election outcome can be more likely
oneLine: A counterexample to Harrison-Trainor's linearity conjecture, the transitive maximum, and what win totals reveal.
abstract: When many voters rank a fixed set of candidates independently and uniformly at random (impartial culture, the standard yardstick of voting theory), the head-to-head majorities form a random tournament, and a cyclic triple (A beats B, B beats C, C beats A) is an instance of Condorcet's paradox. Harrison-Trainor conjectured that, in the limit of many voters, a labelled tournament with fewer cyclic triples is always the more probable one; he checked this for up to five candidates. This candidate shows that the conjecture is false. For every odd t there are tournaments on 14t candidates in which the tournament with 3t³ more cyclic triples is 2^(3t²+o(t²)) times as probable: the probability cost is governed by pairs of candidates whose strengths must be almost equal, while cyclic triples are governed by triples, and ordered block structures make the two disagree. An exact rational certificate gives an explicit pair on 78 candidates: the tournament with three more cyclic triples is more than 10⁵ times as probable, and the reversal persists for isomorphism classes. Monte Carlo computation, which is not a proof, finds no reversal on seven or fewer candidates and finds reversals on 13 and 14 candidates. The extremal half of the conjecture is true: the transitive tournaments are exactly the most probable ones, for every number of candidates and a wide class of paired-comparison models. A second part shows that, outside the Bradley–Terry case, the win totals of a round robin leave exponential differences in probability, which an exactly calibrated triangle test detects from one round robin, and that one observation per pair cannot support the minimax Bradley–Terry–Luce test of Makur and Singh at constant separation; whether a constant number of observations suffices remains open. Limits: impartial culture is a null model, not real elections; the election results are many-voter limits with no finite electorate size; the smallest counterexample lies between 8 and 13 candidates on numerical evidence and is certified at 78. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 4.3 (proof, main): Harrison-Trainor's linearity conjecture is false. For every odd t, the ordered block tournaments with blocks (7t, 7t) and (t, 9t, 3t, t) on 14t candidates differ by 3t³ cyclic triples, and the more cyclic one is 2^(3t²+O(t log t)) times as probable.

Proposition 5.1 and Corollary 5.2 (exact certificate): on 78 candidates, the tournament with blocks (7, 7, 49, 5, 5, 5) has three more cyclic triples (4,943 against 4,940) than the one with two blocks of 39, yet is more than 10⁵ times as probable; for isomorphism classes the ratio exceeds 3.3.

Section 5.2 (Monte Carlo, not a proof): no reversal among all tournaments on up to seven candidates or block tournaments on 8 to 12; reversals on 13 candidates (by about 1%) and 14 candidates (by a factor of about 2.7).

Theorem 6.1 (proof): the transitive tournaments are exactly the most probable labelled tournaments, for every number of candidates and every exchangeable latent-strength model whose win probabilities increase strictly with strength.

Theorem 7.1 and Section 8 (proof): for a fixed comparison model, either the win totals determine every outcome's probability (Bradley–Terry) or a typical outcome shares its win totals with outcomes e^(±cn²) times as probable; triangle tests are exactly calibrated given the win totals and detect every such departure from one round robin.

Proposition 9.1 (proof): with one observation per pair, the minimax Bradley–Terry–Luce test of Makur and Singh is impossible at constant separation; whether a constant number of observations per pair suffices remains open.

narration:
Imagine many voters, each ranking the same candidates in a random order. For every pair of candidates, look at who wins the head-to-head majority vote. Sometimes three candidates form a loop, like rock, paper, scissors: A beats B, B beats C, and yet C beats A, closing the loop. This is Condorcet's paradox, and this random-voter model is the standard yardstick of voting theory.

A natural guess, made as a formal conjecture by Harrison-Trainor, is that an outcome with fewer of these loops is always more likely than one with more. He checked it for small elections, with up to five candidates, and found that it held.

This release shows that the guess is false. Split the candidates into ranked groups, where everyone in a stronger group beats everyone in a weaker group. Each pair of candidates that must end up almost tied costs roughly a factor of two in probability. Loops live inside groups, and so do the costly pairs. But pairs grow with the square of a group's size, while loops grow with its cube, so some arrangements have more loops yet need fewer almost-tied pairs.

An exact certificate gives a concrete case with seventy-eight candidates: an outcome with three extra loops is more than a hundred thousand times as likely. Computer estimates, which are not proofs, find no such reversal with seven or fewer candidates, and they do find reversals with thirteen candidates, and with fourteen, among the cases examined.

Part of the conjecture survives. The fully ordered outcomes, with no loops at all, really are the most likely ones, whatever the number of candidates.

A second part speaks to anyone who analyses round robins, such as a sports season. Unless the Bradley-Terry model holds, the win totals hide a great deal, and a simple test built from triangles of games can detect this from a single season. But with only one game per pair, no test can meet the worst-case standard proposed by Makur and Singh.

The election results are about a mathematical null model with very many voters, not real elections, and the size of the smallest counterexample is still unknown.

This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review and exact computer checks rather than outside peer review, and its proofs, programs and limits are open for anyone to inspect.

Hązła, Mossel, Ross and Zheng (2020), The probability of intransitivity in dice and close elections. Probability Theory and Related Fields. The Gaussian many-voter limit, and close elections, where every tournament is asymptotically equally likely.
Mossel (2010), Gaussian bounds for noise correlation of functions. Geometric and Functional Analysis. The probability that the majority tournament is transitive.
Varin and Firth (2024), Tractable ridge regression for paired comparisons. Stat. The Thurstone–Mosteller model with random strengths, whose marginal likelihood matches the limiting probabilities.
Saile and Suksompong (2020), Robust bounds on choosing from large tournaments. Social Choice and Welfare. Lemma 6 on transitive score vectors, cited and distinguished from the compression theorem.
Chatterjee (2015), Matrix estimation by universal singular value thresholding. Annals of Statistics. Matrix estimation used by the spectral test.
Makur and Singh (2025), Minimax hypothesis testing for the Bradley–Terry–Luce model. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. The replication question answered for one observation per pair.

Rastogi, Balakrishnan, Shah and Singh (2022), Two-sample testing on ranked preference data and the role of modeling assumptions. Journal of Machine Learning Research 23(225). The masking construction (Proposition 4) adapted for the replication result.
Lauritzen (2008), Exchangeable Rasch matrices. Rendiconti di Matematica e delle sue Applicazioni. The characterisation of models whose win totals determine probabilities (Section 2.4).
Iyer (2016), Random tournaments. Honours thesis, Australian National University. Theorem 4.2.9, the same characterisation for tournaments.
Singh and Davidov (2026), Testing for lack of fit in paired comparison data (arXiv:2604.00426). The closest current lack-of-fit tests, for cardinal or replicated data.
